Abstract

When injected in deep saline aquifers or depleted oil and gas reservoirs, supercritical CO2 remains mobile and can, therefore,
migrate through any conduits or fractures. In addition, public opinion, regulations and the lack of space for CO2 injection in
some densely populated regions of the world such as the Japanese archipelago encourage investigating other alternatives such
as carbon dioxide sequestration in deepwater sub-seabed formations.

This paper intends to present a technical feasibility study of CO2 sequestration in deepwater sediments offshore Japan. The
main processes, technical requirements, technologies and structures that are currently available to transport and inject liquid
CO2 successfully in sub-seabed formations below 9,000 feet of water (≈2,750 meters) are first discussed. Then, three storage
sites situated offshore Japan; one located in the Northwest Pacific Ocean near the island of Shikoku; another located in the
Sea of Japan near the island of Honshu; and the last one located farther in the Northwest Pacific Ocean in ultra-deepwater
(18,000 feet); are selected to conduct reservoir simulations.

From this study, it appears that CO2 capturing technologies and transporting means seem to be at a mature stage. Also,
current and newest 5th and 6th generation drilling vessels are estimated to be capable of drilling very shallow wells in water
depths greater than 9,000 feet and even in ocean waters as deep as 18,000 feet if new materials such as titanium or composite
for riser systems were to be deployed for both the drilling and CO2 injection operations. However, CO2 storing and injection
facilities are not available yet to unload large quantities of CO2 offshore. As a result, some concepts should be designed,
qualified and tested for these large scale operations within the next decade to demonstrate through pilot projects the technical
feasibility of CO2 sequestration in sub-seabed geological formations.

Additionally, the main findings from this comparative study and reservoir simulations conducted at three different sites
located offshore Japan confirm that a significant part of ultra-deepwater regions with at least 9,000 feet of ocean water and
planar seafloor are appropriate for CO2 storage. Secondly, reservoir models confirm that due to high pressures and low
temperatures reigning at water depths greater than 9,000 feet, the liquid CO2 injected in the first few hundred feet of
sediments has a higher density than the surrounding formation pore-fluid and therefore remains buoyantly trapped under
certain condition of geothermal gradient, sediments permeability and formation pressure and; hence constitute a valid and
safe CO2 storage candidate.

Introduction

CO2 annual emissions currently account for about 30 billion tons (IEA, IPCC, 2010). In addition, carbon dioxide released in
the atmosphere in the near future, by 2030, is expected to reach at least 40 billion tons emitted annually. Even though almost
half of this greenhouse gas will eventually be absorbed by natural processes (CO2 slowly moved from surface waters of the

Earth’s oceans and seas to deeper waters because the solubility of CO2 in water increases with increasing pressure), the
remaining part of the CO2 may stay in the Earth’s atmosphere for centuries (Marchetti, 1977).

Besides, if one compares the current annual emission of CO2 with the largest offshore carbon sequestration project in the
world where about 1 million tons of CO2 has been injected each year for the last 15 years in the permeable Utsira sandstone
formation in Norway, it becomes evident that a very large number (greater than 10,000) of carbon sequestration projects
utilizing multiple approaches and technologies would be needed to stabilize atmospheric CO2 emission levels.

To date, the bulk of CO2 sequestration studies and pilot projects have focused on capturing the CO2 and injecting it, usually
in a supercritical state, in deep saline aquifers, depleted oil and gas fields or abandoned coal mines where a physical trap
would not allow, in principle, any leakage of the injected CO2. However, at the relatively high pressures and high
temperatures present at these formation depths, the supercritical CO2 becomes buoyant and therefore, can migrate if the
formation is not perfectly sealed. Therefore, any already present micro-fractures or rock property changes due to excessive
CO2 injection pressure or regional tectonics could represent a potential leakage mechanism for the buoyant CO2.

In fact, governments and public opinion would probably be opposed to extensive drilling campaign for injection wells and
CO2 sequestration operations taking place at injection sites located at close distance from populated areas because of the
potential risks of having the CO2 leaking and migrating up the ground surface. Thus, in some densely populated regions of
the world such as the Japanese archipelago which has very little available space for large onshore CO2 sequestration projects,
other alternatives such as injecting and sequestering carbon dioxide in offshore formations must be investigated. In addition,
since there is an intense tectonic activity in Japan, the risk of having buoyant supercritical CO2 leaking from the geologic
formations where it has been injected into is too great and therefore would require a different type of trapping mechanism for
the CO2 such as a gravitational trap where the heavier fluid (i.e. liquid CO2) would remain below the lighter fluid (i.e.
sediments pore-fluid) even though geomechanical perturbations occur.

Since all carbonate species are very dependent on temperature and pressure conditions, other CO2 sequestration
methodologies had to be investigated in order to find a pressure and temperature window where carbon dioxide could be
safely and permanently stored underground. Thus, based on theoretical and experimental works that have taken place over the
last three decades to study whether the Earth’s oceans and marginal seas could sequester anthropogenic CO2 (Nakashiki et al,
1995), it has been found that when liquid CO2 is injected at great water depths, beyond 9,000 ft (≈2,750 meters), CO2 actually
becomes denser than seawater because of the low temperatures (between 35°F and 40°F) and high pressures (greater than
4,000 psi) reigning at these water depths (Fer and Haugen, 2003). However, because deep ocean currents will eventually
transport some of the CO2, which has not dissolved with seawater, to the water surface and eventually release it back into the
atmosphere, a different environment, current-free and with a better trapping mechanism is therefore required to permanently
store the CO2.

Thus, it has recently been proposed that CO2 could be injected just below the seafloor and benefit from the unique pressure
and temperature regimes occurring at these great water depths (House et al, 2006 and 2008, Schrag, 2009). Moreover, since
the International Maritime Organization announced in 2007 that storage of CO2 under the seabed was allowed, injecting and
storing CO2 in deepwater sediments appears as one of the safest and most viable CO2 sequestration option.

In this paper, three ultra-deepwater storage sites with water depths ranging between 9,300 ft and 18,200 ft situated offshore
Japan; one located in the Pacific Ocean near the island of Shikoku; another located in the Sea of Japan near the island of
Honshu and; the last one located farther in the Northwest Pacific Ocean (N40° E150°), are selected to conduct reservoir
simulations. Also, the main processes, technical requirements, technologies and structures that are currently available to
transport and inject liquid CO2 successfully in deepwater sub-seabed formations are reviewed.

CO2 Capture, Transportation and Injection Offshore Japan

CO2 is often captured and separated from several industrial processes but is vented to the atmosphere because of the absence
of rules and the lack of tax incentives. Three main processes are currently used to isolate the CO2 from the industrial gas
stream: pre-combustion, post-combustion and oxy-fuel combustion. For this feasibility study review, both pre-combustion
and post-combustion capturing technologies where the CO2 is separated from the gas stream using a physical or chemical
sorbent are selected as efficient and cost effective methodologies.

For all of these three case studies located offshore Japan, once the CO2 is captured and separated from various industrial
processes such as power generation plants, cement manufactures, oil refineries, iron and steel facilities within the major cities
(Yokohama-Tokyo, Saitama, Sendai, Sapporo, Nagoya, Osaka, Kobe and Kyoto notably), it is then stored momentarily in
large CO2 tanks. Then, carbon dioxide is transported from the different CO2 tanks using onshore CO2 pipelines. CO2
pipelines can carry CO2 in its supercritical phase (CO2 pressure above 1070 psi and temperature greater than 88°F). Due to
pressure drops along the route, recompression stations are needed to maintain the CO2 pressure above 1070 psi if the distance
from the CO2 tanks to the CO2 terminal near shore is too large (≥ 100 miles). Then, once the supercritical CO2 has reached
the terminal, two means of transportation to carry the CO2 from the terminal onshore to the injection vessel offshore
deepwater can be used. First, subsea pipelines lying on the seabed and connecting the subsea injection wellheads to the shore
pipeline terminals. However, deepwater pipelines have not been installed yet in the Sea of Japan and the Northwest Pacific
Ocean and would require significant capital expenditure to build a deepwater CO2 pipeline network. Besides, because of the
very high tectonic activity of the region, this mean of transportation is not identified for the moment as economically viable
for CO2 injection in deepwater formations.
CMTC 151756                                                                                                                     5


CO2 can also be transported by ship which appears to be the best solution for CO2 sequestration in the ultra-deepwater
regions near the Japanese archipelago. Transporting CO2 via ships requires much less capital expenditure than transporting it
through ultra-deepwater pipelines and also provides greater flexibility, thus allowing the CO2 to be conveyed to multiple
injection sites. The ships use semi-pressurized and semi-refrigerated tankers to keep the CO2 in its liquid phase similar to the
ones used to transport liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) or liquefied natural gas (LNG) products and can carry CO2 volumes
over 500,000 ft3 which can allow the injection of more than 100 million tons each year if the CO2 injection site is at relatively
close distance to shore such as the ones located in the deepwater parts of the Sea of Japan or offshore the island of Shikoku in
the Northwest Pacific Ocean. In addition, even in the case of the third injection site located in the Northwest Pacific Ocean
farther from the Japanese nearest shore, at least 10 million tons of CO2 could be injected each year around each site which
would still constitute the largest CO2 sequestration project in the world. In addition, once the CO2 transportation vessel has
reached the injection site, the CO2 can be offloaded using a fluid discharge process similar to the one used with oil tankers
where the CO2 ship is connected to an offshore buoy that is tethered to a submerged turret located in the center of the
injection vessel and where the CO2 is temporary stored before CO2 injection operations can start.

Then, the selection of a drilling, storing and injection structures for operations in the deep waters off the coasts of Japan must
take into account an exhaustive number of parameters to ensure the success of CO2 sequestration in deepwater formations.
The essential criteria to be considered are water depth, metocean conditions (waves, current, wind), operating period (year-
round), offloading and storage of the CO2, injection capability and rate. Currently, in the deepwater industry, semi-
submersible ships (5th or the latest 6th generation) are most often the best suited option when operating in potential rough
water and weather environments such as the Northwest Pacific Ocean and the Sea of Japan because of their better stability in
pitch, roll and heave as compared to ship shaped vessels. In addition, other concepts such as circular shaped vessels that
could perform both drilling and injection operations and that could also store the CO2 after being offloaded from the CO2
transportation ship are currently under development and could provide a more economic alternative (Srinivasan et al, 2008).

Therefore, for the injection operations in the near future, a large 5th or 6th generation semi-submersible vessel is chosen as the
optimum choice to drill a shallow wellbore and inject CO2 in ultra-deepwater sediments of either the Sea of Japan or the
Northwest Pacific Ocean. Although being a major obstacle until recently, drilling and injecting CO2 in water depths greater
than 9,000 ft is within the limits of the deepwater oil and gas drilling industry (the 10,000 ft water depth frontier was passed
in 2003 by one of the latest 5th generation drill-ship in the Gulf of Mexico and the new world record was recently established
offshore India in over 10,200 ft of water in April 2011). Moreover, in order to conduct drilling and injection operations
through over 10,000 of water column, riser type systems need to be employed.

Drilling and injection risers are both key components to ensure the structural and pressure integrity when the drilling fluids or
the injected CO2 are being carried from the vessel floor to the seafloor. Drilling risers can be described as vertical rigid pipes
with added buoyancy modules on the outside and injection risers are flexible pipes, steel catenary risers (SCRs) or composite
material pipes. The design of drilling and injection risers is very critical for these ultra-deepwater CO2 injection operations
because risers undergo repeated external and internal loading from the waves, ocean currents, drilling fluids and injected
liquefied CO2.

Thus, front-end engineering analyses have already been carried out and documented for steel drilling and injection riser
systems for a CO2 sequestration feasibility study in 11,000 feet of water in the Gulf of Mexico (Pilisi et al., 2010) but new
results are provided in Table 1 for different drilling and injection riser configurations (steel risers, titanium risers, hybrid:
steel+titanium risers, slim steel risers and composite injection risers). The results from these static and dynamic analyses are
for a dynamically positioned semi-submersible vessel first located in about 9,000 feet of water off the coasts of Japan as
shown in Table 1 and then for a vessel located in 18,000 feet of water in the Northwest Pacific Ocean as shown in Table 2.

The analyses were segmented for three different environmental loadings (calm, moderate and rough weather conditions) and
show that new riser system materials, notably titanium alloy drilling riser and composite injection riser systems or slim riser
systems made of steel (16 in. diameter instead of 21 in. in diameter), are required to ensure that drilling and injection
operations can be conducted successfully year-round and even during ‘extreme’ weather conditions (100 year event).
However, if the injection site is located in water depths less than 10,000 feet, in a calm weather area, ‘conventional’ steel
drilling and injection riser systems can be deployed to conduct CO2 sequestration operations.

Ultra-deepwater CO2 Injection Well

The injector wells that need to be drilled in the deepwater sediments have to be very shallow wells if the liquid CO2 needs to
remain permanently stored through the presence of a ‘gravitational’ trap (i.e. high pressure and low temperature) within the
sub-seabed formations. Thus, this makes the drilling operations and wellbore design very peculiar and somewhat much easier
as compared to ‘conventional’ deepwater drilling which target is to produce hydrocarbons trapped relatively deep
underground (several thousand feet below the seafloor).

Moreover, the injection of liquid CO2 in the deepwater sediments which is a critical component in the overall success of the
carbon dioxide sequestration process can be achieved by pumping this fluid down through an injection riser and into a cased
wellbore. Thus, the bottom part of the injection casing needs to be perforated to enable the liquid CO2 to enter the sub-seabed
sediments. Also, for these applications, the perforation interval ranges between 10 feet and 30 feet depending on the injection
depth, the permeability of sediments and the thickness of the sediments. In addition, the last casing string or injection casing
can be set either within or just below the zone where the CO2 density is greater than ‘air+seawater’ pore-fluid. Hence, the
injection casing setting depth can range between 300 feet and 3,000 feet depending on the geothermal gradient in the
sediments. In addition, it has been estimated that a 7 inch injection casing could convey CO2 volumes averaging 3,000 tons
per day (i.e. over 1 million tons per year). Besides, once the carbon dioxide leaves the wellbore at relatively shallow depths,
the injection rate that may vary between 1,000 tons per day and 5,000 tons per day creates instantly a pressure increase in the
vicinity of the wellbore, thus, allowing the liquid CO2 to enter the pore-fluid constituted of both the void space and formation
fluids and therefore starting the sequestration process.

CO2 Sequestration in Deepwater Sediments Overall Process

Figure 4 illustrates the entire CO2 sequestration in deepwater sediments process where the carbon dioxide can be captured
and separated from any industrial process and then, once stored temporarily in CO2 tanks, is transported in its supercritical
phase to the nearest shore where it is unloaded to a refrigerated CO2 ship where the CO2 remains in its liquid phase (stage 1
on Figure 4). Then, the CO2 is unloaded offshore to a deepwater floating unit which can be a drilling, storing and/or injection
facility or only composed of a drilling unit for the drilling phase to drill the injection well and; afterward, a storing and
injection unit can move on location to perform the injection operations (stage 2 on Figure 4). At that time, the liquid CO2 is
ready to being injected into the deepwater sub-seabed geological formations using injection riser pipes and can, thus, migrate
within the deepwater sediments through perforations set in the 7 in. injection casing string (stage 3 on Figure 4).

CO2 Injection Site Characteristics

Nevertheless, drilling in an ultra-deepwater environment and injecting CO2 in the first few hundred feet of sediments, to
benefit from a ‘gravitational’ trapping mechanism that ensure that the liquid CO2 will remain sequestered indefinitely
requires that the injection sites be selected cautiously considering a number of critical parameters that may greatly influence
the reservoir engineering viability studies. Thus, the potential well-site locations chosen for this paper should have the
following characteristics and known data:

    a.   Water depth greater than 9,000 feet.
    b.   Sediment thickness greater than 100 feet.
    c.   Geothermal gradient (30°C/km to 120°C/km depending on local heat flow in the deepwater regions).
    d.   Sediment permeability (ranging from a few μD to 100 mD).
    e.   Sediment porosity (ranging from 40% to 90%).
    f.   Nearest port located not too far from the deepwater site (≤ 200 miles).

Since seawater, pore-water fluids and CO2 properties change as a function of depth (i.e. pressure) and temperature, seawater
and geothermal gradients data are critical parameters to be computed in the reservoir models. Thus, based on data from the

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) related to world’s oceans and deep seas temperature and a
breadth of peer reviewed articles and books (Pickard et al., 1990), the mean seawater temperature ranges from 40°F to 80°F
at surface, depending on the latitude and seasons, to an asymptotic value of 35°F-39°F once it reaches about 4,000 feet water
depth, and then, the seawater temperature remains constant down to 9,000-18,000 feet water depth. In addition, as depth
increases, temperature of the sediments is a function of the thermal properties of the rock and regional tectonics and, hence,
changes CO2, pore-fluid and seawater densities.

Extensive literature is available concerning scientific expeditions that have been conducted with the Deep Sea Drilling
Project (DSDP between 1968 and 1983), the Ocean Drilling Program (ODP between 1985 and 2004) and the Integrated
Ocean Drilling Program (IODP since 2004) in order to study the ocean and deep sea basins of the world and notably
numerous boreholes have been drilled, monitored and cored in different deepwater regions of the Sea of Japan and the
Northwest Pacific Ocean around Japan. From the different cores recovered, permeability and porosity data have notably been
measured and have been used for the reservoir simulations detailed in this paper.

Also, detailed studies have been recently been published specifically focusing on geothermal gradient and heat flow data in
the Japan Sea and Northwest Pacific area (Figure 5: Tanaka et al, 2004). Figure 5 shows a wide range in heat flow values of

Reservoir Simulations for 3 Injection Sites Offshore Japan

To model the liquid CO2 plume mobility once it is injected in the sediments, a three dimensional equation of state
compositional reservoir simulator (GEMTM) has been used with the additional greenhouse gas module (GHG). The numerical
simulations have been run after building a three dimensional reservoir model with a 25x25x60 Cartesian grid blocks for
heterogeneous deepwater sediments with the injection well positioned in the center at grid (13, 13) and completed in the
lower grid blocks. Through three case studies taking place in the Sea of Japan (site N°1) and the Northwest Pacific Ocean
(sites N°2 and N°3) as shown in Figure 6, the CO2 is injected in the deepwater sub-seabed formations, at water depths
ranging between 9,300 feet and 18,200 feet, in deepwater sediments located at about 328 feet below the seafloor with a rate
of 5,000 tons per day for 25 years. Then, the injection operations are stopped but the simulations are still run for another 225
years (i.e. 250 years since the beginning of the injection operations). Finally, the results of the numerical models for three
different injection sites show the variations in CO2 concentration in the sediments pore-volume and the immobility or
migration of the CO2 as a function of sediment temperature, pressure, permeability and porosity.

The data used as input in the numerical simulations are petrophysical property measurements of the deepwater sediments that
come from samples that have been collected by the Deep Sea Drilling Project (Pisciotto et al., 1992; Hill et al., 1993) and the
Ocean Drilling Program (Kanazawa et al., 2001) in boreholes located nearby each of the three injection sites. Based on some

geostatistical simulations for the numerical simulations.

Simulation Results

The numerical simulations for site N°1 considers a reservoir constituted of deepwater sub-seabed lithogenous sediments with
basaltic deposits having a total thickness of 328 feet (100 meters) located in the Japan Sea in 9,281 feet of water. The
temperature and pressure at the seafloor are respectively 35°F and 4,150 psi and the average geothermal gradient in the first
few hundred feet of sediments is as high as 6°F per 100 feet. For site N°2, the reservoir is composed of deepwater pelagic
sediments with a total thickness of 328 feet (100 meters) located in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, near the island of Shikoku,
Japan in 9,850 feet of water. The temperature and pressure at the seafloor are respectively 35°F and 4,405 psi and the average
geothermal gradient in the first few hundred feet of sediments is also 6°F per 100 feet. The reservoir simulations for site N°3
also located in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, near the coast of Japan compute a similar reservoir model containing pelagic
sediments with a total thickness of 328 feet (100 meters). However, since site N°3 is located in 18,158 feet of water, the at
the seafloor is greater (8,120 psi) and the geothermal gradient in the first few hundred feet of sediments for this area is much
lower than the previous injection sites with 2°F per 100 feet.

For site N°1, the results of the numerical simulations show the global mole fraction of the injected CO2 in the deepwater
lithogenous sediments after a timeframe of 250 years as shown in the upper part of Figure 7. It can be seen that the CO2
migrates both in the lateral and vertical directions but remains gravitationally trapped within the sediments on the lower part
of the numerical model after some time. Indeed, the relatively high geothermal gradient of 6°F per 100 feet has a direct effect
on the migration of the CO2 plume. Thus, it can be seen that CO2 mole fraction takes values of 1.0 (red color on Figure 7) in
the vicinity of the injection zone representing about 2x2x6 grid blocks. Also, it appears that CO2 concentration values in the
upper and lateral parts of the sediments model are greater than zero which indicates that the CO2 has migrated upward and
then stayed gravitationally trapped in the bulk volume and can, therefore, be considered as immobile (light blue and green
colors on Figure 7). In addition, CO2 mole fraction values in the farthest lateral and the most upper parts of the numerical
model are null which shows that the CO2 has not reached these locations in the sediments even after 250 years, staying
trapped within the pore-volume and, hence, proves the viability of the sequestration method (blue color on Figure 7).

Additionally, the results of the numerical simulations for site N°2 also show the global mole fraction of the injected CO2 in
the deepwater pelagic sediments after a period of time of 250 years. Similarly to the previous reservoir for site N°1, the CO2
migrates both in the lateral and vertical directions because of the relatively high geothermal gradient of 6°F per 100 feet
present within the deepwater sediments; but, as well, remains trapped within the pelagic formations after reaching a
gravitational equilibrium on the bottom part of the reservoir model as illustrated in the middle of Figure 7. Again, CO2 mole
fraction takes values of 1.0 (red color on Figure 7) in the vicinity of the injection zone for a slightly larger volume than for
site N°1, representing about 3x3x7 grid blocks. Likewise, CO2 concentration values in the upper and lateral parts of the
numerical model are greater than zero which indicates that the CO2 plume has moved in the vertical and lateral directions and
then has been gravitationally trapped in the bulk volume (light blue and green colors on Figure 7). Also, CO2 mole fraction
values in the farthest lateral and the most upper parts of the numerical model are null which shows that the CO2 has not
migrated to these locations, remaining immobile within the pore-volume, thus demonstrating the benefit of this carbon
dioxide sequestration solution (blue color on Figure 7).

For the third CO2 injection site, the results of the numerical simulations show the global mole fraction of the injected CO2 in
the ultra-deepwater lithogenous sediments of the Northwest Pacific Ocean after an elapsed time of 250 years (bottom part of
Figure 7). As compared to the two previous numerical simulations, it can be seen that the CO2 has not migrated as much in
both the vertical and horizontal directions remaining trapped for the most part within the sediments. This is can be explained
because of the presence of a relatively low geothermal gradient of 2°F per 100 feet in the rocks, at this location. Thus, CO2
mole fraction is very high values of 1.0 (red color on Figure 7) in the vicinity of the injection zone for a larger volume than
for the previous case studies (sites N°1 and N°2) representing about 4x4x8 grid blocks. Furthermore, CO2 mole fraction
values in the upper and lateral parts of the reservoir model are not null indicating again that the CO2 is trapped within the

Moreover, an additional numerical simulation has been run for the case where CO2 is injected at 3,000 feet below the seabed,
in the deepwater sediments of the Japan Sea (i.e. water depth equals 9,281 feet). However, at these conditions of temperature
and pressure (P=5,450 psi and T=200°F at 3,000 feet) CO2 changes its state from liquid phase to supercritical phase.
Therefore, supercritical CO2 migrates relatively rapidly upwards until changing back its phase from supercritical to liquid;
and finally reaches a depth below the seafloor where the temperature in the sediments is much cooler (≤80°F) than the
temperature at the injection depth (i.e. 200°F) as shown in Figure 8. Hence, at this relatively shallow depth, liquid CO2
becomes gravitationally trapped within the sediments due to its liquid phase density being heavier than the surrounding pore-
fluid density.

Conclusions

Through three feasibility studies located offshore Japan (in the Japan Sea, offshore Shikoku in the Northwest Pacific Ocean
and farther northeast in the Pacific Ocean), the main processes, technical requirements and technologies that are currently
available, or may be needed, to capture, transport and inject the CO2 successfully in deepwater sub-seabed formations have
been reviewed. Thus, both capturing technologies and CO2 transportation by ship are presently at a mature stage. In addition,
drilling shallow CO2 injection wellbores in water depths ranging between 9,300 feet and 18,200 feet are within the capability
of the newest 5th and 6th generation drilling vessels if the main components (i.e. drilling and injection riser systems) are made
of titanium alloys, composite materials or lighter steels. In addition, at the moment storing and/or injection vessels are not yet
available to conduct CO2 injection operations in ultra-deepwater environments.

Additionally, for each of the three CO2 injection sites, results from computer models show that the storage of liquid CO2 as
an immobile fluid gravitationally trapped within the sediments pore-volume is viable because of the conditions of pressures
(high) and temperatures (low) that are present in these deepwater sub-seabed formations when the CO2 is injected relatively
shallow under the seabed. Indeed, the injection depth seems to play a critical role in the mobility of the liquid CO2 once it is
injected into the deepwater sediments as illustrated when carbon dioxide is injected in the deepwater sediments at 3,000 feet
below the seafloor. Thus, at relatively high sediment temperatures (≥80°F), CO2 changes its phase to become supercritical
and therefore has lighter density than the sediments pore-fluid. Hence, the local geothermal gradient value influences greatly
the migration of the CO2 plume in the sediments. Moreover, overall, under certain deepwater sediment parameters (i.e. low
temperature, high pressure, relatively high porosity and permeability), it has been shown in this paper that CO2 sequestration
in deepwater sub-seabed formations is a viable and much safer technique for storing CO2 than the structural cap rock located
on top of an aquifer within which supercritical CO2 is injected into or even when anthropogenic CO2 is injected in depleted
oil and gas fields for storage.

In addition, even though theoretically this CO2 sequestration solution should not be sensitive to any structural geology or
regional tectonics since the denser CO2 stays at the bottom of the ‘air+seawater’ pore volume, more numerical simulations
accounting for geomechanical perturbations will be required to demonstrate the integrity of the gravitational trap in
earthquake sensitive areas such as the Japanese archipelago.
14                                                                                                              CMTC 151756


Furthermore, additional reservoir simulations are required to demonstrate that the injection of liquid CO2 will not change the
ocean chemistry because of the displaced formation fluid present originally within the deepwater sediments. Also, CO2
hydrates formation may act either as an additional trapping mechanism or a limiting factor for CO2 injection and could
therefore extend or reduce the number of potential candidates for CO2 sequestration in deepwater sediments.

Finally, CO2 storage in deepwater sub-seabed formations could be used on a global scale to mitigate greenhouse gas
emissions to permanently store the captured CO2 from various industrial processes; and thus constitute a viable alternative
especially for densely populated areas, seismic sensitive regions such as Japan.
